Learning Objectives
Identify the contents of the individual compartments of the upper and lower extremities.
Describe the typical clinical presentation of chronic exertional compartment syndrome.
Accurately diagnose and provide effective and evidence-based nonsurgical and surgical
treatment for patients with chronic exertional compartment syndrome.
Introduction
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) describes pain and impairment of
neuromuscular function because of increased intramuscular pressure and impedance of blood


Introduction
CECS describes pain and impairment of neuromuscular function as a result of increased
intramuscular pressure and impedance of blood flow because of repetitive loading.
Multiple theories and mechanisms have been suggested as the underlying etiology for
CECS. Symptoms are reversible and characteristically resolve rapidly with cessation of
activity.1 CECS often is initially managed via nonsurgical modalities and rehabilitation;
however, surgical decompression of the fascial compartments frequently is the
subsequent treatment option of choice for active individuals2 (Resources 1, 2 and 3).
Epidemiology
Approximately 95% of patients with CECS have involvement of the lower leg.
CECS is the cause of exertional leg pain in 27% to 33% of patients.
CECS commonly is associated with bilateral symptoms, male predominance, and a peak
prevalence in patients aged 20 to 25 years.
CECS in the forearm is rare.

Epidemiology
Although 95% of patients with CECS have involvement of the leg, CECS has been
reported in the forearm, thigh, and foot.3 Lower-extremity CECS is most often observed
in running athletes and members of the military4 and is the cause of exertional leg pain
in 27% to 33% of patients; however, rates may be as high as 49.5% in some patient
populations.5,6 In military populations, the incidence is estimated at 0.49 cases per 1,000
person-years, with a total case number of 4,100 diagnosed over 5 years.7,8
The peak prevalence of CECS occurs in patients aged 20 to 25 years. CECS is associated
with male predominance, is associated with increasing levels of activity, and frequently is

bilateral.6 Age (20 to 25 years), male sex, bilateral symptoms, previous lower leg
pathology, specific sports (running and skating), and tender muscle compartments are
independent predictors of lower leg CECS.6 CECS of the forearm is rare and occurs in
athletes performing repetitive and vigorous gripping activities, such as in rowing and
cycling9 (Resources 4, 5, 6, and 7).
Anatomy
The forearm is divided into the volar, dorsal, and mobile wad compartments.
The volar compartment is further divided into the superficial, intermediate, and deep
compartments.
The leg is divided into the anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior
compartments.

Anatomy
The forearm is divided into the volar, dorsal, and mobile wad compartments9 (Figure 1).
The volar compartment is further divided into the superficial, intermediate, and deep
compartments. The superficial volar compartment contains the flexor carpi ulnaris,
pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, and palmaris longus. The intermediate volar
compartment contains the flexor digitorum profundus. The deep volar compartment
contains the flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus, and pronator quadratus.
The median and ulnar nerves traverse multiple compartments in the volar forearm. The
dorsal compartment contains the radial nerve, extensor digitorum communis, extensor
digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris, anconeus, supinator, abductor pollicis longus,
extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, and extensor indicis. The mobile wad
contains the brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis brevis, and extensor carpi radialis
longus.9

The leg is divided into the anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior
compartments5 (Figure 2). The anterior compartment contains the tibialis anterior,
extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius, deep peroneal
nerve, anterior tibial artery, and anterior tibial vein. The lateral compartment contains
the peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, and superficial peroneal nerve. The superficial
posterior compartment contains the gastrocnemius, soleus, and sural nerve. The deep
posterior compartment contains the tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor
digitorum longus, posterior tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery, and posterior tibial vein.5

Pathophysiology
True pathophysiology is not entirely understood.
Multiple theories and etiologic factors have been proposed for the pathogenesis of CECS.
Various risk factors also have been suggested.

Pathophysiology
During exertion, muscles expand in volume by as much as 20%.10 This expansion against
noncompliant osseofascial borders increases intracompartmental pressure,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
5/26

compromising local tissue perfusion.11-13 However, the pathophysiology CECS is not
completely understood.8 Although thicker and stiffer fascia has been suggested as an
associated factor, this has not been proven.14,15 Lower capillary density in affected
individuals also has been proposed as an etiologic factor.5,16 Exercise-induced,
osmotically active muscle breakdown products and ischemia-induced increases in
cellular permeability may further increase pressure in the compartment.17 Running
technique, as it relates to transmission of ground reaction forces through the legs,18,19
and water-retentive creatine supplementation also have been suggested as risk
factors.20
The process by which CECS produces symptoms also is unclear. Transient tissue
ischemia, oxygen supply-demand mismatch, compression or stimulation of sensory
fibers within the fascia or periosteum, and incomplete clearance of muscular breakdown
products and metabolic byproducts have all been suggested as reasons for symptom
production.17,20-22
Clinical Features
Symptoms often present after repeatable and predictable periods of exertion and resolve with
rest.
82% of patients present with bilateral symptoms in the lower extremity.
A finding of fascial hernia on physical examination is associated with low sensitivity and
specificity.
Physical examination may reveal firm, taut, and tender compartments; physical examination
after an exercise challenge may increase its sensitivity.

Clinical Features
CECS presentation may vary but typically includes a constellation of exertional symptoms
that resolve with rest. Pain often is described as aching, cramping, or burning and often
will occur after repeatable and predictable periods of exertion. . Among patients with
involvement of the lower extremity, 82% have bilateral symptoms.20 Symptoms usually
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
6/26

resolve immediately after cessation of activity, or within minutes; however, symptoms
may persist for longer durations over time.5,9,17,20 Although distinct entities, prolonged
CECS may progress to acute compartment syndrome if unaddressed.17,20
Physical examination typically is unremarkable because the examination often is
performed with the patients being asymptomatic and at rest. However, post-exertion
physical examination commonly exhibits firm, taut, and tender compartments. The
presence of a fascial hernia is associated with a low sensitivity and specificity,20,23,24 and
provocative testing for compressive neuropathy and vascular examination at rest often
are normal. Therefore, clinicians should perform the physical examination after an
exercise challenge to increase its sensitivity.5,9,20 Associated distal paresthesia and
motor weakness may be observed depending on the specific neurologic structures
within the involved compartments (Table 1). The presentation of CECS may be unclear;
therefore, other etiologies, such as venous thromboembolism, vascular entrapment, or
bone stress injury, must be excluded.

Diagnostic Studies
The diagnosis of CECS is primarily clinical; however, the current preferred diagnostic test is
intracompartmental needle manometry. The modified Pedowitz criteria are most commonly
used; however, other criteria have been described.
Lack of standardization exists in the testing protocol and technique used in performing
intracompartmental needle manometry to diagnose CECS.
MRI and ultrasonography have been used to aid in diagnosis of CECS; however, additional
studies are necessary to determine the utility of imaging studies in the diagnosis of CECS.
Diagnosis of CECS is primarily clinical;3,5,9 however, MRI, ultrasonography, and compartment
pressure testing via needle manometry may aid in the diagnosis if the clinical picture is unclear
(Resource 5).
Intracompartmental Needle Manometry

Intracompartmental Needle Manometry
Measurement of intracompartmental pressure (ICP) is complicated by lack of
standardized protocols, techniques, equipment, and other confounding factors, which
may lead to heterogeneous diagnostic accuracy.25,26 ICP is measured directly with the
use of a slit catheter or a side-port needle manometer.27 Although different proposed
diagnostic criteria have been described, the modified Pedowitz criteria remain the
current preferred diagnostic criteria5,12,24,28,29 (Table 2).

The current literature describes a consistent and reproducible approach for performing
intracompartmental needle manometry of the leg.27 Continuous ICP measurement, as
described in the Roscoe criteria, is uncommon and may be difficult to perform in clinical
practice. Correct catheter placement during intracompartmental manometry ensures
accurate measurements and avoids neurovascular structures in close proximity (Figure
3). Access to the anterior compartment is achieved lateral to the middle third of the tibia
(Video 1); superficial placement is recommended to avoid the neurovascular bundle. The
lateral compartment is accessed with the needle perpendicular to an imaginary line
drawn from the fibular head to the lateral malleolus at the middle third of the leg. Care
should be taken to avoid the anteriorly located superficial peroneal nerve. To access the
superficial posterior compartment, the needle should be slightly medial to the midline
because the saphenous vein, medial sural nerve, and lateral sural nerve lie between the
two heads of the gastrocnemius and the soleus. A medial approach to the deep
posterior compartment is preferred because it avoids the two neurovascular bundles of
the compartment. The needle is inserted at the middle third of the leg just medial to the
medial edge of the tibia in an anterior-to-posterior approach. The flexor digitorum
muscle is entered first, followed by the posterior tibialis muscle, which is confirmed
when a second pop is felt.27 Some clinicians advocate the use of ultrasonography to
guide needle placement; however, comparisons of landmark and ultrasonographic-
guided techniques have not demonstrated benefit.30

Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
MRI has demonstrated increased fluid-weighted signal in patients with CECS after
exercise;21,31-33 however, widespread diagnostic utility of MRI is limited because of lack
of standardized MRI protocols and diagnostic criteria. MRI may be helpful to rule out
alternative diagnoses, such as bone stress injury, soft-tissue injury, and space-occupying
lesions. Ultrasonography is an increasingly popular imaging modality because of its
point-of-care accessibility and low cost. Rajasekaran et al34 demonstrated increased
anterior compartment thickness using ultrasonography in a pilot study of four patients
with CECS; however, additional research is necessary.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
13/26

Nonsurgical management is the first-line treatment option for CECS and should be exhausted
before proceeding with surgical management; however, additional studies are necessary to
determine the effectiveness of specific modalities.

Nonsurgical Management
First-line management of CECS is nonsurgical because of the risks associated with
surgical decompression.3 Initial management may include rest, activity modifications,
NSAIDs, massage, strengthening, stretching, taping, and orthotics; however, evidence on
the effectiveness of these modalities is lacking. Gait re-training, chemodenervation, and
percutaneous ultrasonographic-guided fascial fenestration have been reported to be
beneficial in certain populations that wish to avoid surgical treatment.3 Dry needling and
extracorporeal shock-wave therapy have been proposed as part of a comprehensive
nonsurgical treatment program but have not been extensively evaluated.35
Gait Re-Training

Gait Re-Training
Gait re-training is a common treatment approach for various lower-extremity pain
syndromes and, therefore, has been investigated in the management of CECS. Most
individuals have a propensity to run with a hindfoot striking pattern, which theoretically
increases the load on the anterior and lateral compartments. Targeted gait re-training
aims to decrease this load by changing the running gait to a midfoot or forefoot striking
pattern with some studies favorably showing decreased pain, increased running
distance, and decreased ICP after intervention.3,19,35 Running gait is dependent on many
variables, including stride length, lower-extremity angle, hindfoot angle, ground contact,
shoe type, ground reaction forces, and vertical loading, which make clinical evaluation
and research difficult. The complex interplay of these variables and the possible
introduction of secondary biomechanical adverse effects (eg, increased eccentric loading

9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
14/26

of the calf muscles and the Achilles tendon may predispose patients to tendinopathy)
suggest that more robust gait analysis studies are necessary.35
Chemodenervation

Chemodenervation
In 2013, Isner-Horobeti et al36 described the use of botulinum toxin A to manage
symptoms of CECS. Small amounts of botulinum toxin A may decrease muscle
hypertrophy and, therefore, ICP. Several studies have shown that botulinum toxin A
injections are beneficial in reducing compartment pain and pressure for as long as 9 to
11 months.3,35,37,38 Although promising, additional studies are necessary to determine
the efficacy, proper dosing, and ideal administration protocol to prevent muscle
weakness.
Ultrasonographic-Guided Fenestration

Ultrasonographic-Guided Fenestration
Finnoff and Rajasekaran39 reported a case of fascial fenestration with the use of an 18-
gauge needle under ultrasonographic guidance of the affected compartments. This
novel office-based approach was able to successfully treat a patient with CECS; however,
additional studies are necessary before routine use of this technique.
Surgical Management
Surgical decompression is the definitive treatment option for the management of CECS;
additional studies are necessary before novel minimally invasive treatment options become
widespread.


Surgical Management
Surgical decompression is the definitive treatment option for the management of CECS
and includes traditional open fasciotomy, endoscopic compartment release, minimally
invasive single-incision fasciotomy, percutaneous fasciotomy, and ultrasonographic-
guided percutaneous fasciotomy.4,5,9,40,41 A systematic review and a case series of
surgical outcomes revealed that primary surgical management via open fasciotomy for
CECS was successful in approximately two-thirds of young athletic patients, with 84% of
patients satisfied with results at short-term to midterm follow-up.4,42 Endoscopic
surgical techniques may lead to faster recovery; however, additional studies are
necessary.42 A recent limited systematic review of outcomes of the management of
CECS, including gait re-training, botulinum toxin injection, and fasciotomy, showed
higher rates of satisfaction and return to activity with surgical management.43
Open Fasciotomy

Open Fasciotomy
Open fasciotomy has been the standard approach to release all four compartments of
the leg. A 10-cm incision is initially made between the tibia and fibula on the
anterolateral aspect to release the anterior and lateral compartments. Alternatively, a
two-incision technique can be used to release the anterior and lateral compartments
(Video 2). An additional 10-cm incision is then made medially just posterior to the tibia to
release the deep and superficial posterior compartments4 (Figures 4, 5, and 6). If one
incision is desired, careful dissection to release the superficial and deep compartments
may be performed after the initial anterolateral incision4 (Resources 8, 9, and 10).

Endoscopic Fasciotomy

Endoscopic Fasciotomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
18/26

Recent advancements in endoscopic technology have increased the preference for an
endoscopic surgical approach, especially for the pediatric patient population. A 3-cm
incision is made between the tibia and the fibula on the mid-anterolateral leg to dissect
down to the fascia. Meniscal knives are then used with endoscopic technique to release
the fascia of the anterior and lateral compartments.4 A similar technique is used with a
3-cm incision at the mid-leg at the posterior medial tibia border to release the superficial
and the deep posterior compartments.4 The endoscopic-assisted approach is associated
with efficacy similar to that of open fasciotomy but is associated with an increased risk of
postoperative hemorrhage because the saphenous vein can be damaged with release of
the posterior compartments.4,42
Single Mini-Incision Fasciotomy

Single Mini-Incision Fasciotomy
Traditionally, all four leg compartments would be released in patients with CECS even if
the posterior compartments did not have increased ICP; however, studies have
investigated releasing only the compartments with increased ICP, most commonly the
anterior and the lateral compartments.4 Maffulli et al44 published a study in 2016 on the
use of a single mini-incision to release only the anterior and lateral compartments, with
a 2.5-cm incision made on the anterolateral aspect at the middle third of the leg 1 cm
lateral to the tibia. From this incision, the anterior and lateral compartments were
released with the use of scissors under direct visualization.44 The mini-incision approach
has been shown to be associated with benefits comparable to those of open fasciotomy
reported in smaller studies;4 however, additional research is necessary.
Ultrasonographic-Guided Fasciotomy

Ultrasonographic-Guided Fasciotomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000048
19/26

Finnoff and Johnson40 described a novel minimally invasive fasciotomy performed under
ultrasonographic guidance. With this technique, the fascia of the anterior leg
compartment is transected with ultrasonographic visualization after a 3-mm V-shaped
meniscotome is introduced through a 3-mm incision under local anesthesia. This
minimally invasive approach allows for visualization of nerves and vessels but must be
studied on a larger scale.
